emails.subject: The $120 sitting in your group's closets
emails.preview: Four friends, four copies of Catan, one that gets played. There is a better way to buy.
emails.html:
Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

Picture four friends who meet every other Thursday. Over a year, each of them buys Catan. One copy gets played. The other three sit in closets, still in shrink wrap: about $120 of games nobody opened.

The one idea: a play group needs one copy of a game, not one copy per person. Everything your group owns is one library spread across several homes.

The article walks through the cost-per-play math (say a $40 game played 20 times by four people: about 50 cents per player per play), a table comparing twenty coordinated purchases with twenty uncoordinated ones, the exceptions where a second copy earns its keep, and a six-step plan for starting a Shared Shelf this week.

Try it this week: ask everyone in your group to drop a list or a photo of their games in the chat. Mark every repeat.

emails.subject: The one question before buying a second copy
emails.preview: Sometimes two copies is the smartest buy on your list. Here is how to tell.
emails.html:
Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

The One Copy Rule is easy to agree with. The arguments start at the edges: your kids want the group's Azul on a Tuesday, or a cheap filler would live in your bag.

The one idea: buy a second copy only when it creates plays that would not otherwise happen. Convenience does not count. The urge to own does not count. Plays count.

The article runs that test on each real exception (two separate groups, a home copy, games like Dominion that improve with two sets, the always-played anchor, cheap fillers under about $20), then names the reasons that only sound like exceptions, such as "it was on sale" and "in case they stop coming." It ends with an eight-question checklist.

Try it this week: before your next purchase, name the next three plays that copy will get, with real people and real dates. If you cannot, wait.

emails.subject: Who buys what once you share a shelf
emails.preview: Four friends buying in four directions cover a lot more ground than four chasing the same hits.
emails.html:
Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

Once your group agrees to buy one copy of each game, a new question shows up fast: who buys the next one? Left alone, four strategy fans end up with four shelves of strategy games and nothing for the night a cousin comes to town.

The one idea: each person in the group takes one slice of the library, so purchases spread across genres and player counts by design.

The article lays out six lanes (strategy, party, co-op, 2-player, campaign, filler), a worked example where four friends buying five games each reach 21 distinct games and every player count from two to a dozen, how to assign lanes by taste and hosting habits, and when to rebalance as people join or leave.

Try it this week: ask each person which kind of night they enjoy most, then have everyone write down a first and second choice of lane.

emails.subject: What happens when wine hits the Wingspan board
emails.preview: Eight plain agreements that keep a shared collection from turning into a grudge.
emails.html:
Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

A shared collection runs on trust, and trust holds up better when a few things get said out loud. A missing meeple, a glass of red wine across a board, a friend moving to another city: none of these should end a game group.

The one idea: a Shared Shelf needs a short, plain social contract, agreed once, then forgotten until it is needed.

The article answers the questions groups avoid: big games live where they get played, lost pieces are a group cost, real damage gets an offer to replace and the owner decides, the friend who never hosts contributes another way, the heavy buyer still follows their lane, and games leave with their owner when someone moves. It closes with an eight-line Group Shelf Charter.

emails.subject: The birthday gift that four people get to open
emails.preview: Expansions to the base-game owner turn birthdays and holidays into library building.
emails.html:
Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

Most board game gifts are a coin flip. You guess, and the box either becomes a favorite or joins the Shelf of Shame. One kind of gift almost never misses.

The one idea: give expansions to whoever owns the group's base game. One person receives the gift, and everyone at the table gets to play it.

The article shows why a $25 expansion for a game with thirty plays behind it (an illustration) is one of the cheapest ways to add new play, how to keep a short gift list per person, why a group wishlist stops duplicate gifts and makes a $100 campaign game an easy four-way present, and the etiquette: the gift belongs to the recipient, and sleeves and bags are always welcome.

Try it this week: add a "wants" column to your pooled shelf and have each person name two or three expansions or accessories for games they own.

emails.preview: Two groups, two years, same budget. One finishes with 17 games and 16 spare boxes.
emails.html:
Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

Meet the Maples and the Oaks, two made-up groups of four. Both love games, and both spend about $200 per person per year. The only difference: the Oaks had one conversation in month one.

The one idea: coordination, not budget, decides the size of your library. Same money, same two years, one group ends with about twice the games.

The article follows both groups purchase by purchase. The Maples buy Catan three times in a month and end with about 17 distinct games and 16 spare copies, roughly $640 or 40% of their spend. The Oaks buy in lanes and end with about 34, plus four expansions and a group-funded campaign game. Then it describes a typical night for each group, including the one where a fifth friend shows up.

emails.subject: One box, eight players, no one buys anything
emails.preview: What a Magic Cube proves about shared libraries, even if you never touch a Magic card.
emails.html:
Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

One person brings one box. Eight people draft decks from it, play for three hours, and put every card back. Next week the same box produces eight completely different decks.

The one idea: a Magic Cube is the One Copy Rule at its limit. One curated copy, kept by one person and played by many, is not a compromise. It is the better version of the hobby.

The article explains a Cube in plain terms for anyone who has never played Magic, runs it through the cost-per-play formula, and pulls out three lessons for any board game group: curation beats accumulation, one caretaker per library, and rotation keeps one copy fresh. It also visits our Magic Cube community in Indianapolis, relaunching as part of The Ludarium.

Each person in your group knows their own shelf, and maybe the three games a friend always brings. Almost nobody has written the whole library down in one place. One evening and one table fixes that.

emails.subject: The best first game purchase is nothing
emails.preview: Where to play for free, and the 90-second log that keeps wrong buys off your shelf.
emails.html:
Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

Most collections start backward. A box catches your eye, you buy it, and then you find out it needs four players when you usually have two. The game goes on the shelf and stays there.

The one idea: spend your first few months at other people's tables, game cafés, and the library, and buy only once you already know you like a game. The $0 tier is where every good library starts.

The article lists the free tables most people overlook, gives you a taste log to copy (mechanic, real length, player count, who you played with), and shows how skipping three wrong buys in a year saves roughly $100. The surprise: after loving a game at a friend's house, the right move is often to keep playing it there.

Try it this week: after your next play, take 90 seconds to log the mechanic, the real time including the teach, the count, and who was there.

emails.subject: Your first $40 is not for your favorite game
emails.preview: A four-quality scoring rubric and anchor candidates for couples, families, and crowds.
emails.html:
Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

Your favorite game might be a three-hour engine builder. Buying it first is how a lot of shelves get their first unplayed box.

The one idea: the anchor is one game, about $40, chosen for the table you really have rather than the one you imagine. Get it right and everything you add later has something to attach to.

The article names the four qualities that predict plays (fits your usual player count, teaches in 10 minutes, survives repeat plays, you would be proud to bring it), scores them in a rubric where 16 or higher is anchor material, and lists candidates by situation: Patchwork for couples, Ticket to Ride for families, Catan for four or five, Codenames for a crowd. It also covers what not to buy first: heavy strategy, campaign games, and anything on a Kickstarter timeline.

emails.subject: Six games, six jobs, under $300
emails.preview: Gateway, filler, 2-player, party, co-op, stretch. One each, and no two in the same role.
emails.html:
Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

After a year of buying on impulse, a lot of people own four 90-minute strategy games for four players. From the table's point of view they are the same game, and on the night eight people show up, the shelf has nothing.

The one idea: a starter shelf is six games in six roles (gateway, filler, 2-player, party, co-op, stretch), and no two games fill the same role. Built that way, it covers nearly every night you host.

The article walks through what each role has to do, gives a sample shelf that lands around $180 to $230 at typical retail, and sets the buying order: gateway first, filler second, stretch last, on purpose. It also shows how four friends who coordinate share twenty-four distinct games instead of four copies of Catan.

Try it this week: write the six roles on an index card and mark which ones your shelf, or a friend's, already covers. The biggest gap is your next purchase.

emails.subject: Where does your group actually play?
emails.preview: From $300 to $1,000: first expansions, cost per play, and buying with a person's name on it.
emails.html:
Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

Once six games cover six roles, "what am I missing?" stops being the useful question. Your play log has months of evidence now, and it probably says one role gets most of the plays.

The one idea: at the core library stage you go deeper where your group already lives and resist going wider everywhere else. The article's rule of thumb: 70 percent of spending goes to the two roles you play most.

It covers when a first expansion is worth it (15 or more logged plays and a group asking for variety), how to start tracking cost per play (as an illustration, a $40 game played 20 times is $2 a play, 50 cents a seat at four players), buying for a specific person, and a table of when a second game in a role earns its place.

emails.subject: Past $1,000, the question is what it replaces
emails.preview: A shelf cap, one in one out, buying used first, and the annual review that keeps a shelf honest.
emails.html:
Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

Somewhere past $1,000 the shelf is full. Every new box pushes an old one out or lands on the floor, and the collection becomes something you manage, not something you build.

The one idea: the people who do this well think like curators, not collectors. Set a shelf cap, and for every game that comes in, one goes out the same week.

The article explains why the cap works (a 60-game collection and a 25-game collection get about the same plays a year, just spread thinner), buying used first for anything over $40, the curator's rule for Kickstarter (name today the game it will replace), and an annual review with three questions per game. One line to keep: can you say in one sentence what this game completes?

Try it this week: pick your cap. The article suggests 30 to 50 games for most people. Then name the one game you would send out first.

emails.subject: The games still on the table in 20 years
emails.preview: Durable, teachable, scales in count, evergreen. Plus why to keep the games your kids outgrew.

Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

Think of the deck of cards at your grandparents' house, or the taped-up box your family played at the lake, one piece replaced with a button. Nobody picked those games on purpose. They lasted anyway.

The one idea: the lifetime library is choosing that deliberately. Of the 30 or 50 games a curator keeps, maybe eight or ten will still be played in two decades, and those deserve the best shelf and a replacement copy while they are in print.

The article names the four qualities that make a game last (durable, teachable across ages, good at two and at six, evergreen), with Carcassonne, Catan, Ticket to Ride, Codenames, and Pandemic as modern examples. It also covers thinking in decades: keep outgrown games for the next kids, and teach your kids to teach, not just to play.

emails.subject: The only board game math worth doing
emails.preview: Price, plays, players, hours: one formula, and the step that does most of the work
emails.html:
Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

Every game has two prices. One is on the shelf tag. The other is what it costs you once you count how often it gets played, how many people sit down, and how long each night runs.

The one idea: cost per play is price ÷ plays ÷ players ÷ hours. It turns a purchase into a rate, so a $15 card game and an $80 box can be compared fairly.

The article walks through each division with one illustration (say a $40 game played 20 times by 4 players for an hour: about 50 cents per person per hour), compares three made-up games in a table, shows why ÷ players matters most and ends with a five-question checklist to run before buying.

Try it this week: estimate plays, players, and hours for one game on your wishlist before you look at the price. Under about a dollar per player-hour is healthy.

emails.subject: The most expensive game you own is unplayed
emails.preview: Why games stall, a 20-minute shelf audit, and three options for every sealed box
emails.html:
Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

Somewhere in your house there is a box still in shrink wrap. Divide what you paid by the hours it has given you, which is zero, and that is the priciest thing on the shelf.

The one idea: price is not where the money goes. Plays are. The surest way to lower what the hobby costs is to stop owning games you do not play.

The article names the four reasons games stall (too heavy, wrong player count, bought on hype, nobody will teach it), gives a 20-minute shelf audit built on three questions, and lays out the only three moves for an unplayed box: schedule it, trade or sell it, or admit you are keeping it. Feeling bad is not on the list.

emails.subject: A ballgame vs. a board game, per hour
emails.preview: The numbers favor the table by a wide margin, as long as one thing stays true
emails.html:
Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

Ask someone who just dropped $80 on a big box whether board games are an expensive hobby and you get one answer. Ask again after that box has carried a dozen game nights and you get another.

The one idea: per person per hour, board games are among the cheapest in-person entertainment there is, because you pay once and reuse the evening instead of renting it.

The article starts from one verified figure: a ballgame for a family of three runs about $130 to $135 for roughly three hours, about $15 per person per hour. It runs a $40 game through the same family, adds movies, a concert, and streaming to the table, and then the catch: a game played zero times loses to everything.

The one idea: your annual number only means something next to the hours it produces. Set it from your plays, not your wishlist, and treat it as a ceiling.

emails.subject: Why that game costs more than last year
emails.preview: Tariffs, thin margins, and the three numbers in the formula you still control
emails.html:
Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

The game you have been eyeing costs more than it did a year or two ago. You are not imagining it.

The one idea: most components are made in China, and US tariffs since 2025 have raised the cost of importing them. Publishers run on thin margins, so it reaches the shelf. But price is one of four numbers in cost per play. The other three are yours.

The article explains why the effect lasts through 2026 and why publishers cannot absorb it, then gives five ways to keep cost per hour low: play before you pay, buy used, share one copy across the group, favor card games, and wait for reprints. A $40 game that becomes $48 goes from about 50 to 60 cents per person per hour, if it gets played.

Try it this week: ask whether anyone in your group already owns the next game on your list. If so, the price increase on it is zero.

A game played twenty times in a stranger's dining room plays exactly like one played twenty times in yours. The only difference is the price.

The one idea: Buying used is how your group gets its one copy for the cost of a couple of lunches, and the only skill it takes is knowing what to check before the money changes hands.

emails.subject: Have you seen the edges of the base game?
emails.preview: Four kinds of expansion, one test to run before buying, and who in the group should own it.
emails.html:
Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

An expansion is the easiest purchase in the hobby to justify. You already love the game, and the box promises more of it. Then a game you played every month becomes one you set up twice a year.

The one idea: An expansion is worth it once your group has played the base game enough to see its edges: the openings feel familiar, the variety repeats, and someone at the table has asked for more.

The article sorts expansions into four types (more players, more content, new mechanics, fixes), shows when a $30 expansion beats a $40 new game on cost per play, names the traps (bloat, buying for the collection, buying for a game you only play at a friend's house), and ends with a six-question checklist and one group rule: the expansion lives with the base-game owner.

emails.preview: Two tests for any campaign page, plus the one-backer rule that keeps a group's money sane.

Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

A campaign page has a countdown, stretch goals, and the worry that the exclusives vanish on the last day. None of that is worth anything at the table a year from now, when the box finally shows up.

The one idea: Picture the game at your local store at its eventual price, with reviews published and your friends' opinions in. If you would not buy it then, you are backing a feeling, not a game.

The article weighs the real upsides (games that would not exist otherwise, backer-only extras) against delays, no reviews of the final game, the deluxe upsell, and shipping and tariff surprises billed later. Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

Everyone has a system for getting games. Almost nobody has one for letting them go, which is how a carefully chosen $300 shelf turns into a $1,000 wall where nobody can find anything.

The one idea: Every used game someone buys is a game someone else decided to move. Learning to be that someone keeps a collection alive instead of merely large.

Two signals flag what goes: not played in a year with nothing scheduled, or the wrong player count for your group. Offer it to your play group first, then local swap groups, math trades, store consignment, and online marketplaces, in that order. emails.subject: A con plan for buying games you will play
emails.preview: A gap list, the demo-first rule, a 24-hour pause, and one buyer per game across your group.
emails.html:
Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

Hundreds of booths, every game demoed by someone enthusiastic, exclusives gone by Sunday, friends buying all around you. No place is better at sending you home with a game you play once.

The one idea: Regret starts before the con. Walk in with a gap list from a shelf audit, play before you pay, and let only one person in your group buy each game.

The article covers writing the gap list as roles, not titles (“a co-op for four that plays in under an hour”), setting a budget as a number, the demo-first rule and its two exceptions, a 24-hour pause for anything over about $60 as an illustration, why most exclusives are cosmetic, and how to get the haul home without crushed corners.

Try it this week: Do a quick shelf audit with your group and write three gaps as roles. Keep that list for the next con, and agree on who buys what before the doors open.

emails.subject: Pick a number and never own more than that
emails.preview: How to choose your cap, how a new game earns its slot, and the once-a-year cull.

Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

A shelf of thirty games gets played. A shelf of a hundred and thirty gets browsed. Past a point, every new box buries one you love.

The one idea: A shelf cap turns “do I want this?” into “is this better than something I already own?” That higher bar is what makes buying well automatic.

The article gives four ways to pick your number (shelf space, roles, a year of plays, your collection tier). Then the mechanics: name the outgoing game before you buy, make the new one beat the weakest game on the shelf, count expansions as part of the base game, and move the out pile within a month. It closes with a four-question annual cull and how a group splits one cap by lane.

Try it this week: Count the distinct games your group actually played in the last year. Set a cap a little above that, lower than feels comfortable, and name the first game that would go.

emails.preview: Where to find players, how often to meet, and what the first three sessions should look like.

Most new game groups do not fail because the games were bad. They fail because dinner was ambiguous, the night ran until 1 a.m. on a Wednesday, and "whenever we can all make it" turned into a chat nobody posts in.

The one idea: a play group needs a room, a few games, and people who will show up on the same night twice in a row. Fix the night, play with whoever comes, and build the shelf as a group from day one.

The one idea: rotating the host rotates the shelf. Each home holds a different lane, so a simple rotation puts the whole library on the table over a year without anyone hauling a tote bag, and it turns every member from guest into curator.

The article gives you the simplest possible schedule (a fixed list, the next three dates pinned, swap rather than skip), the host-versus-guest split, why the host picks from their own lane, four standing roles for the member who cannot host, a sample eight-week month, and fixes for the four ways rotation breaks.

You read about a brilliant four-hour game and picture your friends leaning over the map. Two years later it has been played once, by three of you, and one of them left at the halfway point.

The one idea: a game's value is created at the table, not on the shelf. Buy for your group's real player count, real play window, and real appetite for rules, because groups are stubbornly themselves.

emails.subject: Sort your shelf by the job, not the box
emails.preview: Seven roles, one afternoon, and a shelf a guest can read from the doorway.
emails.html:
Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

Big boxes on the bottom, small boxes piled on top. It looks tidy and it tells you nothing. So at 7 p.m. with four people in the living room, you scan the whole shelf and land on the same three games again.

The one idea: shelve your games by the role each one plays on game night, not by box size. A role-based shelf answers "what do we have for tonight?" in seconds, and it shows you where you keep buying the same thing.

The article lays out the seven roles (gateway, filler, 2-player, party, co-op, stretch, campaign), a four-step afternoon to re-shelve everything in labeled zones, a sample layout for a 20-game bookcase, and a test: a friend at the door should pull a reasonable pick for any scenario in under thirty seconds.

Try it this week: tape the spines of your ten most-played games with the role, the player count your group really uses, and the real play time: "FILLER / 3-5 / 15 min." Twenty seconds a game.

emails.subject: What did your group actually play last month?
emails.preview: Five fields, fifteen seconds a night, and in three months your shelf tells the truth.
emails.html:
Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

Ask a gamer for their favorite games and you get a confident list. Ask what they played last month and the list gets shorter and quieter. A lot of money disappears into that gap.

The one idea: a play log shows the difference between the collection you imagine and the collection your table actually uses. Buy from the second one.

The article covers three ways to keep the log (a notebook on the shelf, a shared spreadsheet, or an app), the five fields worth recording (game, date, players, real minutes, and a yes or no on playing it again), and what three months of data hands you: your real top five, real play time, real player count, and every game with zero plays. It also shows how the log feeds cost per play and a one-in, one-out shelf cap.

Try it this week: put a small notebook next to the games before your next game night and write one line per play. Log at the table or within a day; after 24 hours, a play usually never gets written down.

emails.subject: Give every game on your shelf a call number
emails.preview: Role, weight, players, minutes, style: five facts that fit on a strip of tape.
emails.html:
Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

A library can hand you one book out of tens of thousands in two minutes because every book carries a short code. A game box gives you "2-5 players, 30-60 minutes" and leaves out the parts that decide whether tonight goes well.

The one idea: give each game a one-line code built from five dimensions, so two people who have never seen each other's shelves can compare them in a text message.

The five: role on game night (one letter, G for gateway through M for multi-session), weight from 1 to 5 scored for your group rather than from the box, the player range you really play, real minutes including setup, and interaction style (versus, allied, or teams). Pandemic comes out as C2 2-4 45 A. The article then shows how a merged list of codes from four friends exposes duplicates, missing roles, weight ceilings, and length gaps.

Try it this week: code five games on painter's tape, then look at which first letters are missing. That is your next purchase.

emails.subject: Four friends, one library, one spreadsheet
emails.preview: Pool your shelves into a shared list and nobody buys a second Catan again.
emails.html:
Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

Four friends who play every week do not have four collections. They have one library stored in four places. Since nobody can see it, everyone keeps buying as if the other three shelves did not exist.

The one idea: pool every member's games into one shared list. The moment it exists, "should I buy Azul?" turns into "do we already have Azul?"

The article gives a group shelf five jobs (pool the collections, flag duplicates, assign lanes, answer "who has it?", and route expansion wishes to whoever owns the base game) and hands you a spreadsheet template that does all five: a collection tab with one row per copy and columns for owner, role, real players, real minutes, where the box lives right now, lane owner, and status, plus a wishlist tab keyed by base game with a "fills a gap?" column.

Try it this week: start the sheet. Add your own games, one row per copy, then send the link to your group and ask everyone to add theirs. Sort by title and count the duplicates.
